div.ab: [4.a] On sumen lande is, þæt he sceal wyrcan to wicweorce II dagas swilc weorc, swilc him man tæcð, ofer geares fyrst ælcre wucan, ⁊ on hærfest III dagas to wicweorce ⁊ of Candelmæsse oð Eastran III; gif he aferað, ne ðearf he wyrcan ða hwile ðe his hors ute bið. [4.1] He sceal syllan on Michaeles mæssedæig X gafolp'. ⁊ on Martinus mæssedæg XXIII systra beres ⁊ II henfugelas, on Eastran an geong sceap oððe II p. [4.1a] ⁊ he sceal licgan of Martinus mæssan oð Eastran æt hlafordes falde, swa oft swa him to begæð. [4.1b] ⁊ of ðam timan, ðe man ærest ereð, oð Martinus mæssan he sceal ælcre wucan erian I æcer ⁊ ræcan sylf þæt sæd on hlafordes berne; [4.1c] toeacan ðam III æceras to bene ⁊ II to gærsyrðe; gyf he maran gærses beðyrfe, ðonne earnige ðæs, swa him man ðafige; [4.2] his gauolyrðe III æceras erige ⁊ sawe of his aganum berne. [4.2a] ⁊ sylle his heorðpænig. [4.2b] ⁊ twegen ⁊ twegen fedan ænne headorhund. [4.2c] ⁊ ælc gebur sylle VI hlafas ðam inswa[ne], ðonne he his heorde to mæstene drife.

In quibusdam terris operatur opus septimane duos dies sic opus, sicut ei dicetur, per anni spatium omni septimana, et in Augusto III dies pro septimanali operatione et a festo Candelarum adusque Pascha III; si aueriat, non cogitur operari, quamdiu equus eius foris moratur. [4.1] [4.1] Dare debet in festo sancti Michaelis X d. de gablo et sancti Martini die XXIII et sestarium ordei et II gallinas, ad Pascha I ouem iuuenem uel II d. [4.1a] Et iacebit a festo sancti Martini usque ad Pascha ad faldam domini sui, quotiens ei pertinebit. [4.1b] Et a termino, quo primitus arabitur, usque ad festum sancti Martini arabit unaquaque septimana I acram et ipse parabit semen in horreo domini sui; [4.1c] ad hęc III acras precum et II de herbagio; si plus indigeat herbagio, arabit proinde, sicut ei permittetur. [4.2] De aratura gabli sui arabit III acras et seminabit de horreo suo. [4.2a] Et dabit suum heorðpenig. [4.2b] Et duo et duo pascant unum molossum. [4.2c] Et omnis geburus det VI panes porcario curie, quando gregem suum minabit in pastinagium.

On sumen lande is þæt he sceal wyrcan to wicweorce II dagas swilc weorc swilc him man tæcð, ofer geares fyrst ælcre wucan, and on hærfest III dagas to wicweorce and of Candelmæsse oð Eastran III; gif he aferað, ne ðearf he wyrcan ða hwile ðe his hors ute bið. [4.1] He sceal syllan on Michaeles mæssedæig X gafolpæniga, and on Martinus mæssedæg XXIII systra beres and II henfugelas, on Eastran an geong sceap oððe II pæniga. And he sceal licgan of Martinus mæssan oð Eastran æt hlafordes falde, swa oft swa him to begæð. And of ðam timan ðe man ærest ereð oð Martinus mæssan, he sceal ælcre wucan erian I æcer and ræcan sylf þæt sæd on hlafordes berne. Toeacan ðam III æceras to bene and II to gærsyrðe; gyf he maran gærses beðyrfe, ðonne earnige ðæs, swa him man ðafige. [4.2] His gauolyrðe III æceras erige and sawe of his aganum berne. And sylle his heorðpænig. Twegen and twegen fedan ænne headorhund. And ælc gebur sylle VI hlafas ðam inswane, ðonne he his heorde to mæstene drife.

Auf manchem Landgut gilt, dass er über den [ganzen] Jahreslauf hin in jeder Woche zwei Tage als Wochenfrohn solche Arbeit, wie ihm zugewiesen wird, leisten muss; und in der Ernte drei Tage als Wochenfrohn; und von Lichtmess [2. Februar] bis Ostern drei; wenn er Spanndienst leistet, braucht er die Zeit, da sein Pferd draussen ist, nicht zu arbeiten. [4.1] Er muss an Michaelis Festtag [29. Sept.] 10 Zinspfennig zahlen und an Martinus’ Festtag 23 [lies 24?] Sextar Gerste und zwei Hennen, zu Ostern ein Jungschaf oder 2 Pfennig. [4.1a] Und er muss von Martinus’ Fest bis Ostern bei des Herrn [Vieh]hürde [als Wächter] liegen, so oft wie [die Reihe] an ihn kommt. [4.1b] Und von der Zeit an, da man zuerst [im Herbst] pflügt, bis Martinus’ Fest muss er in jeder Woche 1 Acker pflügen und [dazu] das Saatkorn selbst in des Herrn Scheune erholen; [4.1c] ausserdem 3 Äcker [pflügen] als ‘Geheissarbeit’ und 2 als Heu[entgelt]-Pflügen; wenn er weiteren Heus bedarf, dann verdiene er dies, wie man ihm verstattet. [4.2] Als sein Pachtpflügen pflüge er 3 Äcker und besäe [sie] aus seiner eigenen Scheune. [4.2a] Und er zahle seinen Herdpfennig. [4.2b] Und je zwei und zwei [Bauern] müssen einen Hochjagdhund füttern. [4.2c] Und jeder Bauer gebe sechs Laib Brot dem Domänen-Schweinehirten, wenn dieser seine Herde zur Mast treibt.

[4a] On some estates it holds that he must do two days' week-work each week throughout the [whole] year, such work as is assigned him; and three days' week-work at harvest; and three from Candlemas [2 February] to Easter; if he does carrying service [for the lord], he need not work while his horse is out. [4.1] He must pay 10 rent-pence on Michaelmas [29 September], and at Martinmas 23 [read 24?] sesters of barley and two hens, and at Easter a young sheep or 2 pence. [4.1a] And from Martinmas to Easter he must lie at the lord's [cattle-]fold [as watchman] as often as [his turn] comes. [4.1b] And from the time when ploughing first begins [in autumn] until Martinmas he must plough 1 acre each week [for the lord] and himself fetch the seed from the lord's barn; [4.1c] besides that, [plough] 3 acres as boon-work and 2 as grass-[rent] ploughing; if he needs more grass, let him earn it as [the lord] allows him. [4.2] As his rent-ploughing let him plough 3 acres and sow [them] from his own barn. [4.2a] And let him pay his hearth-penny. [4.2b] And every two [geburs] must feed one hunting-hound. [4.2c] And let every gebur give six loaves to the lord's swineherd when he drives his herd to the mast.

In some estates [the custom] is that he must work [for] two days in each week, [doing] such work as he is directed to, throughout the year, and to work [for] three days each week during the harvest, and for three [days each week] from Candlemas to Easter. If he supplies horses for team-work, he need not work while his horses are out. He must pay ten pennies tax on Michaelmas day, and on the day of Martin’s Mass [he must give] twenty-three sesters of barley, and two hens; at Easter [he must give] a young sheep or two pennies. And from Martin’s Mass to Easter he must remain with the lord’s fold as often as it comes around to him. And from the time when one first ploughs to Martin’s Mass he must plough one acre each week, and collect the seed himself from the lord’s barn. In addition to that, [he must plough] three acres as compulsory service on demand and two [acres] pasturage-ploughing. If he needs more grass then he may earn it in such way as one allows him to. His plough-rent [is] to plough three acres and to sow [it with seed] from his own barn. And [he] pays his hearth-penny. As one of a pair [he must] feed a hunting dog. And each peasant pays six loaves to the lord’s swineherd when he drives his drove [of pigs] to woodland-pasture.

On some estates, he is to labor two days each week doing such work as he is directed, and over the harvest he is to work three days a week, and three days a week from Candlemas to Easter; if he is acting as a messenger, he does not need to work while his horse is out in the fields. [4.1] On Feast of Saint Michael, he must pay rent of ten pennies, and twenty-three sesters of barley and two hens on the Feast of Saint Martin, and a young sheep or two pennies at Easter. And from the Feast of Saint Martin to Easter, he must watch over his lord’s sheepfold as often as his turn comes to him. And from the first plowing until the Feast of Saint Martin, he must plow one acre each week and get the seed himself from his lord’s barn. In addition to that, he must plow three acres as mandatory labor and two for pasturage. If he requires more pasture, then let him earn it in an appropriate manner. [4.2] As plow dues, he is to plow three acres and sow it from his own barn. And he should pay his hearth penny. And he should share with another the cost of feeding one hunting hound. And each tenant farmer is to give six loaves to the lord’s swineherd when he drives his herd to pasture.
div.note: This row combines Liebermann's 4a–4.2c. Liebermann would correct ‘XXIII’ to ‘XXIIII’ (preference for multiples of twelve; the last I in the archetype probably resembled ⁊, which B read as a deletion and the Quadripartitus as ‘et’). B's ‘ræcan’ was unclearly altered in chalk to ‘ræfan’ or ‘ræpan’ (not, as editors read, ‘rædan’). Thorpe alters ‘erige’ following the Quadripartitus, wrongly given the genitive. The ‘7’ before ‘twegen’ was later erased. B reads ‘inswa’; Liebermann prints ‘inswa[ne]’. K: double spaces removed.; AU: corrected against Rabin p. 318, October 2026 (was “∅”, now “[4.1]”); AV: corrected against Rabin p. 318, October 2026 (was “∅”, now “[4.1]”); AY: corrected against Rabin p. 318, October 2026 (was “∅”, now “[4.1]”); AZ: corrected against Rabin p. 318, October 2026 (was “∅; ∅”, now “[4.1]; |”); T: corrected against Gobbitt, Early English Laws, RSPandGerefa 4.1, October 2026 (was “heorðpænig . twegen 7 twegen”, now “heorðpænig . 7 twegen 7 twegen”)
This row holds several of Rabin’s sections (4.1, 4.2), each marked with its number.
sesters: A sester is a dry measure of grain equivalent to approximately twelve bushels, or a liquid measure of honey or wine of between twenty-four and thirty-two ounces.
[4.2] plow dues: A tax levied based on the number of plows owned by a householder; typically one penny per plow.

emend to XXIIII, because of the preference for the number twelve; cf. VI in the preceding note and below 5, 1. 8. In the archetype the last I probably resembled ⁊, which B misunderstood as a deletion and Quadripartitus as et

Vgl. Gl Fron 3. Sogar 3 Tage wöchentlich front die Viertelhufe zu Peterborough; Chron. Petrob. [o. 3, 3¹] 158
Cf. Gl Fron 3. At Peterborough the quarter-hide even owes week-work on 3 days a week; Chron. Petrob. [above 3, 3¹] 158

The kind of work, not its duration, is at the lord's discretion; servitium quod praecipiebatur Domesday; cf. Vinogradoff Villain. 298

þa ceorlas sculan dón to Hysseburnan æt hilcan hiwisce (Hufe) 40 penega to herfestes emnihte; Birch 594 also genau wie hier, da 1 ‘Rute’ = ¹/₄ Hufe; s. u.³
þa ceorlas sculan dón to Hysseburnan æt hilcan hiwisce (hide) 40 penega to herfestes emnihte; Birch 594, thus exactly as here, since 1 ‘rod’ = ¹/₄ hide; see below ³

Termin (o. 3⁸) für Kirchenpfennig; s. d. Gl 4a. Dieser ist wohl hier gemeint. Hennen als Kirchenpfennig auch Neilson Custom. rents 195; Haskins in Mél. Bémont 82.—Da Gewicht und Mass von den Zahlen 3 und 4 beherrscht sind, scheint ‘24’ Sextar (s. d. Gl) zu emendieren. Schmid bevorzugt mit Recht gegen Kemble die Lesung B vor Q.—Die Gerstenabgabe ist weit niedriger in Stoke bei Hurstbourne; Bi 594 o.¹

Due date (above 3⁸) for church-penny; see that word in Gl 4a. This is probably what is meant here. Hens as church-penny also in Neilson Custom. rents 195; Haskins in Mél. Bémont 82.—Since weight and measure are governed by the numbers 3 and 4, ‘24’ sesters (see that word in Gl) seems the right emendation. Schmid, against Kemble, rightly prefers the reading of B to that of Q.—The barley render is far lower at Stoke by Hurstbourne; Bi 594 above ¹
æt hiwisce to eastran 2 ewe; ⁊ we [talað] 2 geong sceap to ealdsceapan; ebd. Also hierin trägt wieder die Hufe viermal soviel wie nach Rect die Rute; s. o.¹.—Zum Preise des Schafes s. u. 9

æt hiwisce to eastran 2 ewe; ⁊ we [talað] 2 geong sceap to ealdsceapan; ibid. So in this too the hide again bears four times as much as the rod does according to Rect; see above ¹.—On the price of the sheep see below 9

Schuppen für Schaf, Rind und Pferd (vgl. Toller s. v. fald) lagen oft dem Hofe fern, also durch Diebe gefährdet. Stallbesorgung liegt hierin nicht (gegen Leo), auch nicht soca faldae; vgl. Gl Hürde 3. 4

Sheds for sheep, cattle and horses (cf. Toller s. v. fald) often lay far from the farmstead and were thus exposed to thieves. Care of the stalls is not implied here (against Leo), nor is soca faldae; cf. Gl Hürde 3. 4
[domini] 4 acras debet seminare de semine domini bei London im 12. Jh.; Hale (o. 2⁸) 42. Ggs. u. 4, 2: of his agenum berne
[domini] 4 acras debet seminare de semine domini near London in the 12th cent.; Hale (above 2⁸) 42. Contrast below 4, 2: of his agenum berne

ræcan, gesichert durch 446 Sp. 1{b}, gleich ger- ‘erreichen’, also Gegenteil von gebringan, mit dem es Toller 781a Z. 3 v. u. gleichsetzt; nicht zu verwechseln mit racian. Vgl. Scargill-Bird Cust. of Battle p. 155: Nativi (Gutsbauern) qui carucam habent debent querere semen ad granarium domini, et terram quam araverint debent inde seminare. Aus ungenauem parabit und rædan falscher Lesart übersetzt ‘sorgen’ Schmid, ‘bereiten, herrichten’ Leo, ‘to prepare?’ Toller.—Der Korrektor in B meinte mit ræpan vielleicht die Bed. des jetzigen provinziellen to rape (‘binden’ passt nicht)

ræcan, secured by 446 col. 1{b}, equals ger- ‘to reach’, and is thus the opposite of gebringan, with which Toller 781a l. 3 from bottom equates it; not to be confused with racian. Cf. Scargill-Bird Cust. of Battle p. 155: Nativi (estate peasants) qui carucam habent debent querere semen ad granarium domini, et terram quam araverint debent inde seminare. On the basis of the inaccurate parabit and the false reading rædan, Schmid translates ‘provide’, Leo ‘prepare, make ready’, Toller ‘to prepare?’.—The corrector in B perhaps meant by ræpan the sense of the present dialectal to rape (‘bind’ does not fit)

Die Ergänzung folgt aus yrðe drei Wörter weiter. Nicht ‘auf Nachsuchen als Precarie überlassene Äcker’ (Leo). Ben ist die [ursprünglich ausserordentliche, bei Arbeitsnot erfolgende] Aufforderung, der Befehl zur Fron, im Ggs. zur und neben der ordentlichen Wochenfron, doch ebenso hofrechtlich fest; s. Wb: benierð, benfeorm [precaria quae dicitur ben ad cibum domini; Hale (o. 2³) lxvi. lxxiij; falsch ‘bean-feast’ Toller Suppl. 78], benrip. Vgl. Gl Fron 3; Vinogradoff Vill. 281; Cunningham Henley p. x; Andrews Manor 159; Neilson Ramsey 83. Die Etymologie blieb noch dem 13. Jh. bewusst.—‘Einen Acker in jedem der drei Felder’ versteht Rhamm Grosshufen 723.—Unrichtig bere (‘Gerste’) Schmid

The supplement follows from yrðe three words further on. Not ‘acres granted on request as precaria’ (Leo). Ben is the [originally extraordinary, issued when labour was short] summons, the order to perform labour service, as distinct from and in addition to the regular week-work, yet just as firmly fixed by manorial custom; see Wb: benierð, benfeorm [precaria quae dicitur ben ad cibum domini; Hale (above 2³) lxvi. lxxiij; wrongly ‘bean-feast’ Toller Suppl. 78], benrip. Cf. Gl Fron 3; Vinogradoff Vill. 281; Cunningham Henley p. x; Andrews Manor 159; Neilson Ramsey 83. The etymology was still understood in the 13th cent.—Rhamm Grosshufen 723 understands ‘one acre in each of the three fields’.—Schmid wrongly bere (‘barley’)

Nicht ‘gepflügtes Land’ heisst ierð, wie Toller deutet, und nicht ‘Grasland’, wie Kemble, Schmid, Sweet meinen, an Umbrechen von Wiesenland denkend, als ob ‘und’ = ‘oder’ wäre und to ‘bei, im Falle von’ bedeutete.—Vgl. o. 2⁴. In Ramsey faciet unam aruram, pro illa habebit pasturam, ‘corresponding to graserth of other chartularies’; Neilson Ramsey 41; dies. Custom. rents 70. Greserthe wird mehrfach als ein über den Gemeindeanteil hinausgehendes Recht auf Viehfutter in Wiese und Weide erklärt und heisst daher auch aver-erde (‘Arbeitsvieh-Pflügen’); Vinogradoff Villain. 280f.

ierð does not mean ‘ploughed land’, as Toller interprets it, nor ‘grassland’, as Kemble, Schmid and Sweet think, having in mind the breaking up of meadow land, as if ‘and’ = ‘or’ and to meant ‘at, in the case of’.—Cf. above 2⁴. At Ramsey faciet unam aruram, pro illa habebit pasturam, ‘corresponding to graserth of other chartularies’; Neilson Ramsey 41; the same author, Custom. rents 70. Greserthe is explained several times as a right to fodder for cattle in meadow and pasture going beyond the common share, and is therefore also called aver-erde (‘ploughing with draught animals’); Vinogradoff Villain. 280f.

Nicht ‘seine 3 Äcker Zinsland’ Leo. Auch Schmid, Robertson, Sweet missverstehen ierð als Land. Vielmehr ‘to plough as gafol’ Andrews Manor 158; gavilherth steht als Überschrift in Gutsurkk. über der Angabe, wieviel jeder Hintersass auf herrschaftlicher Domäne pflügen muss; Vinogradoff 280. In Stoke müssen die ceorlas æt ilcan hiwisce . . . III æceras geerian on heora agenre hwile [d. i. nicht als ben oder Wochenfron] ⁊ mid heora agenan sæda gesawan (Birch 594) in Ggs. zu 4, 1b¹. Villani seminant 6 acras de proprio semine; Domesday I 174b 1

Not ‘his 3 acres of rent-land’ Leo. Schmid, Robertson and Sweet also misunderstand ierð as land. Rather ‘to plough as gafol’ Andrews Manor 158; gavilherth appears as a heading in estate records above the statement of how much each tenant must plough on the lord's demesne; Vinogradoff 280. At Stoke the ceorlas æt ilcan hiwisce . . . III æceras geerian on heora agenre hwile [i.e. not as ben or week-work] ⁊ mid heora agenan sæda gesawan (Birch 594), in contrast to 4, 1b¹. Villani seminant 6 acras de proprio semine; Domesday I 174b 1

Mehrere Bauerhöfe verbinden sich auch sonst zur Erfüllung Einer Fron, namentlich beim Pflügen; Vinogradoff 252.—Für herrschaftliche Jagdhunde sorgen die Leute auch in Deutschland und dem Norden; Heyne Nahrung 223

Elsewhere too several peasant holdings combine to perform a single labour service, especially in ploughing; Vinogradoff 252.—In Germany and the North too the people look after the lord's hunting dogs; Heyne Nahrung 223
Da heahdeor ‘Hirsch’ heissen kann, versteht ‘staghound’ Kemble. Vgl. Gl Hund 1 D. 3
Since heahdeor can mean ‘stag’, Kemble understands ‘staghound’. Cf. Gl Hund 1 D. 3
Jagdbeihilfe-Lasten des Untertanen für den Herrn im 11./12. Jh. sammelt Andrews Manor 227
Andrews Manor 227 collects the obligations of subjects to assist the lord in hunting in the 11th/12th cent.

Das präfigierte in- bezeichnet Domäne im Ggs. zum Bauerdorf auch in inheord 7. [Viel zahlreicher sind Composita mit in- als erstem Gliede in der Bed. ‘Hof, Inneneigen, Gutsbezirk’ im Ggs. zur Aussenwelt.] Swan hat hier den Sinn Schweinehirt, da Mast darauf folgt.—Für ‘Herrenhof’ setzt curia Q auch u. 7. Er unterstellt mit dem Worte nicht, dass der Vogt dort Hallengericht (s. d. Gl) hielt (gegen Andrews Manor 138)

The prefix in- denotes the demesne as opposed to the peasant village in inheord 7 too. [Far more numerous are compounds with in- as first element in the meaning ‘court, inner property, estate district’ as opposed to the outside world.] Swan here has the sense ‘swineherd’, since mast follows.—Q also puts curia for ‘lord's court’ below 7. By this word he does not imply that the reeve held a hall-moot (see that word in Gl) there (against Andrews Manor 138)
